---
title: "Combining Generators: Pairs Before Totals"
---

Two dice land on the table. Before we add anything, the observation is a pair.

Keeping that pair for one more moment makes the rest of the calculation visible.

## 🔰 Build the joint possibilities {#sec-sample-combining-generators-build-the-joint-possibilities}

Let $D_1,D_2$ be independent fair six-sided dice. Their possible ordered pairs are

$$
(a,b),\qquad a,b\in\{1,\ldots,6\}.
$$

There are $6\cdot6=36$ pairs. Independence and fairness give each pair probability $1/36$.

The square arrangement is the joint space. Its rows can identify the first face and its columns the second.

A different relationship between the dice could assign different weights to the same square. The square lists possibilities; the joint law weights them.

## 🏵 Choose what the observer keeps {#sec-sample-combining-generators-choose-what-the-observer-keeps}

If we record $Y=h(D_1,D_2)$, several pairs may produce the same recorded value.

For each $y$, collect their masses:

$$
\mathbb P(Y=y)
=
\sum_{\substack{a,b\\h(a,b)=y}}
\mathbb P(D_1=a,D_2=b).
$$

This is an induced distribution. The transformation groups outcomes according to the observation rule.

The word *pushforward* names this transport of a probability law through a function. The dice give us its mechanism before we need the general abstraction.

## ⚙️ The sum and the maximum collect different groups {#sec-sample-combining-generators-the-sum-and-the-maximum-collect-different-groups}

For the sum, the counts at values $2,3,\ldots,12$ are

$$
1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 4,\ 5,\ 6,\ 5,\ 4,\ 3,\ 2,\ 1.
$$

Each count is divided by 36 to obtain probability.

For the maximum, the counts at values $1,\ldots,6$ are

$$
1,\ 3,\ 5,\ 7,\ 9,\ 11.
$$

Why the odd numbers? There are $m^2$ pairs with both faces at most $m$. Remove the $(m-1)^2$ pairs with both below $m$, leaving

$$
m^2-(m-1)^2=2m-1.
$$

```{python}
#| label: fig-sample-pair-maps
#| fig-cap: "The sum and maximum are different maps of the same 36 pairs. Each lower profile counts cells sharing one output value."
#| fig-alt: "Two six-by-six grids show pair sums and maxima. Bar charts show triangular sum counts and increasing odd maximum counts."
#| fig-format: svg
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 7

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

faces = np.arange(1, 7)
pair_maps = [
    (np.add.outer(faces, faces), "Sum", "#236B8E", "Blues"),
    (np.maximum.outer(faces, faces), "Maximum", "#A54B30", "Oranges")
]
figure, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(9, 7), layout="constrained")
for column, (grid, title, color, palette) in enumerate(pair_maps):
    axis = axes[0, column]
    axis.imshow(grid, origin="lower", cmap=palette, alpha=0.4, extent=(0.5, 6.5, 0.5, 6.5))
    for row, first_face in enumerate(faces):
        for col, second_face in enumerate(faces):
            axis.text(second_face, first_face, str(grid[row, col]), ha="center", va="center")
    axis.set(title=title, xticks=faces, yticks=faces, xlabel="Second die", ylabel="First die")
    values, counts = np.unique(grid, return_counts=True)
    axes[1, column].bar(values, counts, color=color)
    axes[1, column].set(xticks=values, xlabel="Recorded value", ylabel="Pair count")
    axes[1, column].grid(axis="y", alpha=0.15)
    axes[1, column].set_axisbelow(True)
plt.show()
```

## 💡 The observation map and the joint weights are separate {#sec-sample-combining-generators-the-observation-map-and-the-joint-weights-are-separate}

Suppose the second die is an exact copy of the first: $D_2=D_1$. Each individual die still has a uniform marginal law, but only the six diagonal pairs occur.

Their sum is one of $2,4,6,8,10,12$. The triangular profile is gone because the joint law changed.

A list of marginal profiles therefore cannot always determine the law of a combined value.

The next pages separate two further operations: [Mixtures](mixtures.qmd) choose a source, while [Convolution](convolution.qmd) calculates the sum of independent sources.

For two independent fair dice, compare the events “maximum at least five” and “sum at least ten.” Explain each count in the square of pairs.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Work it through {#sec-sample-combining-generators-work-it-through}

The first includes $36-4^2=20$ pairs, giving $5/9$. The second includes the six pairs producing totals 10, 11, or 12, giving $1/6$. The same joint generator has been observed through two different maps.
